May Vāta, Mātariśvan, blow auspiciously for us; may Sūrya shine auspiciously for us. May the days be auspicious for us, and may the night be ordained as auspicious. May Uṣas dawn auspiciously upon us, and may Āditya rise for our welfare. O Sarasvatī, be gracious, most peaceful, and full of healing for us.
May it not be visible to you from the sky.
You are the abode for *iḍā*; may we be possessed of an abode; may we not fall away from our abode. May he who hates us and whom we hate be without an abode.
You are the firm foundation; may we be possessed of a firm foundation; may we not fall away from our foundation. May he who hates us and whom we hate be without a foundation.
O Vāta, blow hither the medicine; O Vāta, blow away whatever is harmful. For you, possessing all medicines, move as the messenger of the gods.
These two winds blow from the ocean and from the farthest distance. (89)

[4-42-2] May one wind blow skillfully for me, and may the other blow away whatever is harmful. O Vāta, that storehouse of immortality which is placed in your house yonder—grant us from that so that we may live; grant us from that the healing medicine.

Then may the great wind blow toward us, bringing medicine—beneficent and healing to our hearts—and may it prolong our lives. You are the house of Indra; I enter you along with my cows and horses, together with whatever belongs to me. I take refuge in *bhūḥ*, I take refuge in *bhuvaḥ*, I take refuge in *suvaḥ*, I take refuge in *bhūrbhuvassuvaḥ*. I take refuge in Vāyu; I take refuge in the unafflicted deity; I take refuge in the unbroken stone; I take refuge in the Brahman-treasury of Prajāpati; I take refuge in the Brahman; I take refuge in *Oṃ*.
May the atmosphere be my wide, vast, and lofty interval; may the fires and the mountains, and that well-being by which the wind [blows], with that well-being may my vital breaths be well.

O Prāṇa and Apāna, protect me from death; O Prāṇa and Apāna, do not abandon me. May Agni bestow splendor upon me, may he bestow wisdom upon me, may he bestow progeny upon me. May Indra bestow sensory power upon me, may he bestow wisdom upon me, may he bestow progeny upon me. May Sūrya bestow radiance upon me. 90.

[4-42-3] O Aśvins, protect us with your unharmed blessings day and night. May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this. With what aid will the wonderful, ever-prospering friend come to us? With what most powerful host?

Which true one among the exhilarations will most bountifully intoxicate you with the soma-juice? He who breaks open even the firmest wealth for us. Be, then, the protector of us, your friends and singers, with a hundred aids.
The youthful Suparṇas, the Priyamedha seers, have approached Indra with their supplication:
"Dispel the darkness, fill our eyes with light, and release us like those bound in a snare. (91)
May the divine Waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drinking; may they flow toward us with peace and well-being.
Rulers of precious things, sovereigns over all people.
I beg the waters for healing.
May the waters and the plants be friendly to us; may they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate. For you, O waters, are indeed sources of bliss; grant us strength.
For the great battle, so that we may see [you],
grant us a share here of that most auspicious sap of yours, like longing mothers.
Let us go readily to that [sap] of yours, for whose abode you quicken us.
O Waters, give birth to us.
The Earth is peaceful; she is pacified by Agni; may she, being pacified, appease my burning pain.
The intermediate space is peaceful; it is pacified by the wind; may that peace of mine pacify my afflictions.
The sky is peaceful; it is pacified by the sun; may that peace of mine pacify my afflictions.

The earth is peace, the atmosphere is peace, the sky is peace, the quarters are peace, the intermediate quarters are peace; fire is peace, wind is peace, the sun is peace, the moon is peace, the stars are peace; the waters are peace, the herbs are peace, the trees are peace; the cow is peace, the goat is peace, the horse is peace, man is peace; the sacred word (*brahman*) is peace, the Brahmin is peace; peace indeed is peace—may there be peace for me, may there be peace!
With that peace, with all-encompassing peace, I create peace for myself, for my bipeds, and for my quadrupeds; may there be peace for me, may there be peace!

May Fortune, Modesty, Fortitude, Austerity, Intelligence, Stability, Faith, Truth, and Dharma—these follow me as I rise up; may Fortune, Modesty, Fortitude, Austerity, Intelligence, Stability, Faith, Truth, and Dharma not abandon me.

With long life, with good life, with the essence of herbs, and with the vigor of Parjanya, I have risen up after the immortals. That eye, beneficial to the gods, the bright one, has risen in the east.

May we see for a hundred autumns; may we live for a hundred autumns; may we rejoice for a hundred autumns; may we delight for a hundred autumns; may we exist for a hundred autumns; may we hear for a hundred autumns; may we proclaim for a hundred autumns; may we remain unconquered for a hundred autumns; and may we long behold the sun. 93.
May that Sūrya, the wise one with red eyes, the bull who has risen from the great ocean, from the midst of the shimmering flood, purify me with his mind.

You are the dripping of the Brahman; you two are the poles of the Brahman; you are the receptacle of the Brahman. By the Brahman this great earth is supported; by it the vast mid-air is supported; it supports the sky and the earth together with the gods. What I know, may I maintain that; let my knowledge not fall away from me.
May wisdom and intelligence enter me from all sides for the attainment of what has been and what is to be. May I attain a full span of life; may I attain a full span of life.

O Lord of the Bay Steeds, increasing through these songs, fill up whatever is deficient in us here. When you burst open the great enclosures for the sake of your praisers, then may we be those who receive the greatest portion of your bounty.
We have spoken of Brahman; may it not desert us. Om. Peace, peace, peace. 94.
May he place [us] from afar; may you quicken those who are bound so that they may see—[and there are] seven [verses]. 42.

Homage! They yoke the vigorous steed; O Brahman, with the *pravargya* rite, O Brahman, we shall proceed. Ten eastern [fingers] I beheld as the guardian of the god’s ocean. For the sake of the sacrifice, swell up, O *gharma*! Of those that are great, four bones are in front. Seven for the vital breaths, three for Pūṣan, four for Uda, eleven for those that are yours. Seven for Agni. Sit down, thou who art firm! Nineteen [bones] are in the belly. Thirty upwards from the earth. May the earth be in me! Sixteen are those that are terrible. Nine are *snik*. *Dhuni* and two, and *ugra*.

Three days and nights; five, six, three, seven, seventeen; the earth-faced one has four; that which is this *vṛka* has five; that which is impelled has four; O long-faced one, three; likewise four; that which is these beings has six; having stretched out, three; by the three-eyed one, ten; today by Brahman, six; six, six, eight; the earth has sixty-eight; may there be peace for us; fifty-seven; forty-two. 42.

Homage to Speech! O Brahman, through the Pravargya rite, may radiance be in me; through the intermediate space, you are our father among the great ones. Come near to us! Since this is the earth, [may there be] ninety-four [verses] with the heavens. 94.
[[4-0-0]] Homage! May they be pleased with me.
Oṃ! Peace, peace, peace.
May it be auspicious for us; may it not forsake us. Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.

[5-1-1] The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session (*satra*), desiring glory measured by their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). They said: "Whatever glory shall first reach us, let that belong to all of us together. For them, Kurukṣetra was the altar (*vedi*); its southern half was the Khāṇḍava forest, its northern half was Tūrghna, and its rear half was Parīṇaj.
The Maruts are the rubbish heap. || 1 ||
Yājña seized their sacrifice, which was dedicated to Viṣṇu. He desired that [sacrifice] for himself;
by means of it, he departed.

The gods followed him as they sought glory together. As he was pursued, the bow was born from his left side and the arrows from his right. Therefore, the bow and arrows have a holy birth; for their birth is indeed from sacrifice.
[5-1-3] While he was alone, many did not dare to attack him. Therefore, many who are unarmed do not dare to attack a single man armed with a bow. He smiled.
"Lest others, being many, should overcome me while I am alone. As he smiled, his vital energy departed from him.
The gods deposited it in the plants; they became *śyāmāka* grains. These are indeed called *smayākā*. 3.

[5-1-4] Therefore, there is smiling for those who smile. For that reason, even one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*) should smile while holding [his breath], for the sake of maintaining his vital energy (*tejas*).
He stood there, having braced his bow.
Those earth-worms said, "Let us choose a boon: we shall subject this earth to you;
wherever we dig, there we shall pierce through to the water. Therefore, wherever earth-worms dig, they pierce through to the water.

they even ate his bowstring.

As his bowstring flew forth, it struck off his head; that [head] rolled along heaven and earth. Because it rolled forth (*prāvartata*), that is the reason for the *pravargya* being called *pravargya*.
When he cried out "Yad ghrāṃ," it fell down; that is the reason for the *gharma* being called *gharma*.

as great as the sacrifice is,

for from that part of his [the animal] is what is fit for sacrifice. They go forth surrounding them, to drive away the Rakṣases.
Many carry [the earth];
they bestow honor upon it.
They place it on a raised spot strewn with sand and enclosed by a fence for the sake of peace. He sprinkles it with boiling water.

Or rather, these [stones] are not things upon which one can subsist;
he thus afflicts them with grief. He mixes them with gravel for the sake of stability.
And furthermore, for the sake of peace,
he mixes goat’s hair;
this indeed is the beloved body of Agni.
Because it is a goat, he unites him with his very own dear body.
Then, with splendor,
he mixes it with the hair of the black antelope skin;
for the black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice.
By means of sacrifice alone, he brings forth sacrifice. || 20 ||

One should not offer [the oblation] before the *yājyā* verse; "The bamboo has entered for the sake of peace," he says; "The fivefold [verse] brings prosperity," he says; it carries away, it anoints, it strides forth, it enters, it causes those being born to flow forth—for the sake of peace; and there are eight. 2.
He performs [the rite] in an enclosed space;
for the securing of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

One should not breathe out while performing [an action]. If one were to breathe out while performing it, one would afflict the vital breaths with impurity. One breathes out after having set aside [the action], for the protection of the vital breaths.
One should not pass between the Pravargya and the Āditya [vessel]. If one were to pass between them, one would become afflicted with skin disease.

bamboo is indeed brilliance.

Therefore he says thus:
"You two are the feet of the sacrifice," he says.

moreover, it is for stability.

The meters are indeed vigor. By means of vigor, he thus makes him.

"May you be easy of access to me; do not harm me," he says, for the sake of non-harming. "You are piled, you are piled around," he says;

The Pravargya is indeed the head of the sacrifice.
Now, that Pravargya is truly the sun, and the Maruts are its rays.
"Svāhā! With the Maruts, enclose it! he says.
He thus encloses that very Sun with its rays. Therefore, yonder Sun is enclosed by its rays in yonder world; therefore, the king is enclosed by his subjects.
Therefore, the village chief is surrounded by his own kinsmen;
for when Agni was created,
the splendor (bhās) that he attained was the *vikaṅkata* tree.
In that the enclosing-sticks are made of *vikaṅkata* wood, he wins radiance;
there are twelve of them. || 38 ||
Twelve months are a year; he thus secures the year itself. "There is a thirteenth month," they say.
(Taittirīya Āraṇyaka)

In that there is a thirteenth enclosing-stick, by that very means he wins the thirteenth month. He says, "Thou art the interior of the atmosphere," for the sake of distinction. He places a piece of gold above [the altar], saying, "Protect the sky from heat," so that it may not be over-burnt.
Thus, by means of these two [verses], he encloses him on both sides.
"Worthy, you carry arrows and a bow," he says. || 39 ||
[5-4-11] He thus praises it. "Thou art Gāyatra, thou art Traiṣṭubha, thou art Jāgata," with these words he takes up the fans; he takes them up by means of the meters.
He shakes it, saying, "Honey! Honey!
Honey is indeed breath;
he thus bestows breath upon the sacrificer.
They go around three times;
for the vital breath is threefold.
They go around three times.
The sacrifice increases by threefold repetition. || 40 ||
[5-4-12] Moreover, for the sake of striking away the Rakṣases, they go around three times again. They amount to six; there are six seasons;
verily, they find support in the seasons.
He who indeed steps upon the dear body of the Gharma becomes one with a diseased skin. He who, having gone around three times, goes around a fourth time, truly steps upon his dear body.
It was this [skin] that Ugradeva Rājani removed from him.
From that, indeed, he became afflicted with skin disease.
Therefore, having gone around three times, one should not go around a fourth time.
For the protection of oneself;
the fans are indeed the vital breaths;
they fan without interlacing them.
For the non-intertwining of the vital breaths and for the sake of fulfillment,
they sit down separately and shake [the fire];
thus they become firmly established in the quarters.
They shake it upwards for the attainment of the heavenly world;
they shake it in every direction.
Therefore, he purifies everything from all sides. || 42 ||
He recites [the verses] as if placing them down; this is the blessing at the end of the sacrifice.
They establish another [verse]; they become rays; "on the bow," he says, for the sake of the sacrifice's progress and for completeness—two and [four]. 4.

Taittirīya Āraṇyaka – Searchable Text, Page 92 of 155 – 25.11.2005 – www.sanskritweb.net/yajurveda [[5-5-1]] "May Agni cause thee to shine in the east with the Vasus, by means of the Gāyatrī metre," he says. Verily, Agni causes him to shine in the east with the Vasus, by means of the Gāyatrī metre. "Shining himself, may he cause me to shine," he says.
He utters this very blessing:

"May Indra cause you to shine from the south with the Rudras, by means of the Triṣṭubh metre," he says. Indeed, Indra causes him to shine from the south with the Rudras, by means of the Triṣṭubh metre. "Having been made to shine, may he cause me to shine," he says.
He utters this very blessing.
"May Varuṇa cause you to shine from the west with the Ādityas and with the Jagatī metre," he says. Verily, Varuṇa causes him to shine from the west with the Ādityas and with the Jagatī metre.
"May he find pleasure in me; may I find pleasure in him," he says. He thereby invokes this very blessing.

"May Dyutāna Māruta with the Maruts cause thee to shine from the north by means of the Anuṣṭubh metre," he says. Thus Dyutāna Māruta with the Maruts causes him to shine from the north by means of the Anuṣṭubh metre. "Shining, do thou cause me to shine," he says;
verily, he thereby invokes this blessing.
"May Bṛhaspati with all the gods cause thee to shine from above by means of the Paṅkti metre," he says. Thus Bṛhaspati with all the gods causes him to shine from above by means of the Paṅkti metre.
"May he find pleasure in me; may I find pleasure in him," he says.
He thereby invokes this very blessing. || 44 ||
"O God, you have been made radiant; you are the Gharma among the gods," he says, for he has indeed been made radiant among the gods. "May I be radiant among men," he says.

"He indeed shines among men. "O Emperor, you have shone as the *gharma* among the gods; may you be long-lived, radiant, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*)," he says. For he has indeed shone among the gods; he becomes long-lived, radiant, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge.

"May I become one who has shone among men, long-lived, radiant, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge," he says. He indeed becomes one who has shone among men, long-lived, radiant, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge.

"You are brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me; may brilliance be in me," he says. He thus invokes this very blessing. If, without having caused it to shine by means of these sacrificial formulas (*yajus*), one were to announce, "The *gharma* has shone," the sacrifice would be devoid of luster.
The sacrificer is one who desires radiance. Now, when he has caused him to shine by means of these sacrificial formulas (*yajus*),
he says, "The *gharma* has shone."
The Adhvaryu priest is one who delights;
the sacrificer is one who delights. || 45 ||
Afterwards, he chooses [the verse] with the Jagatī metre; "May he choose me, may I choose him," he says—verily, he thus invokes this blessing. There are eight [verses]. || 5 ||
Taittirīya-Āraṇyaka - Searchable Text, Page 93 of 155 - 25.11.2005 - www.sanskritweb.net/yajurveda [[5-6-1]] This,
indeed, is the head of the sacrifice.
The Pravargya is the head; the Upasads are the necks.
He performs the Pravargya before the Upasads; thus he restores the head of the sacrifice to the necks themselves.
He applies the ointment three times;
these worlds are three.
From these very worlds he secures the head of the sacrifice. They amount to six.
There are six seasons. || 46 ||

[5-6-2] Verily, from the seasons he secures the head of the sacrifice. He draws the Pravargya twelve times. Twelve months are a year; verily, from the year he secures the head of the sacrifice. They amount to twenty-four; there are twenty-four half-months.
Verily, from the half-months he secures the head of the sacrifice. Moreover, it should indeed be consecrated only once; for the head is one.
[5-6-3] He chooses the priests at the Agniṣṭoma;
for the sacrifice is of such extent.
As great as the Agniṣṭoma is,
so great is the sacrifice;
he thereby restores its head.
One should not undergo initiation at the Ukthya sacrifice. The Ukthas are indeed offspring and cattle; were one to undergo initiation at the Ukthya, [he would lose them].
It would burn away his offspring and cattle;
therefore, he applies [the fire] during the Viśvajit sacrifice when all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras are performed.

[5-6-4] The *pṛṣṭha* stotras indeed cause that which is unshakable to fall. By means of the *pṛṣṭhas*, he causes that which is unshakable to fall for him and secures it. "I have seen the Guardian," he says.
The breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the Guardian.
He extends the vital breath among the creatures.
"I have seen the herdsman," he says;
for yonder sun is indeed the herdsman.
He indeed protects these creatures;
he makes him the protector of the creatures. "Without falling down," he says. || 49 ||
Taittirīya-Āraṇyaka - Searchable Text, Page 94 of 155 - 25.11.2005 - www.sanskritweb.net/yajurveda [[5-6-5]] For he does not lie down.
"Moving hither and thither along the paths," he says;
for he indeed moves hither and thither along the paths. "Clothing himself in those that meet and those that diverge," he says.
"Clad in those that flow together and those that flow apart, he gazes upon all creatures; he moves to and fro within the worlds," so it is said. For indeed, he moves to and fro within the worlds.
"Here you have been brought forth by Madhumādhvī and Madhumādhūcī," he says. Thus he prepares for him the two seasons of spring.
"Agni has gone together with Agni," he says. || 50 ||

He thus prepares for him the two summer seasons. "Agni has united with Agni," he says; for this very Agni unites with Agni. "Svāhā! Agni has united with fervor," he says; this has already been explained. He recites the subsequent verse as an accompaniment:
"Supporter of heaven, thou shinest through the mid-air and the earth. He thus prepares for him the two rainy seasons.
"For the heart thee! For the mind thee! he says;
verily, he prepares for him the two autumnal seasons.

"May the *hotrā* offerings rest among the gods in heaven," he says. By means of the *hotrā* offerings, he unites these worlds. "Lord of all beings," he says; he thus prepares for him the two winter seasons (*haimantika*). "O divine Gharma, you who are heard by the gods, protect the gods," he says; he thus prepares for him the two dewy seasons (*śaiśira*).
"Bestow upon us speech born of fervor that yearns for the gods," he says. That which is indeed the speech fit for sacrifice—
She is born of austerity;
verily, he wins her. || 52 ||

“He is the embryo of the gods,” he says; for he is indeed the embryo of the gods. “The father of thoughts,” he says; for offspring are indeed thoughts, and he, the Pravargya, is their father; therefore he speaks thus. “The lord of creatures,” he says; for he is indeed the lord of creatures. “The thought of the sages,” he says. (53)
Taittirīya-Āraṇyaka - Searchable Text, Page 95 of 155 - 25.11.2005 - www.sanskritweb.net/yajurveda [[5-6-9]] For he is the thought of the seers.

"The god has united with the god Savitṛ; he has united with Sūrya, the radiant one," he says. Thus he unites yonder Āditya and the Pravargya and brings them into harmony. "O Gharma, you are the giver of life to us; you are the giver of splendor," he says. He thereby invokes this very blessing. "You are our father; be mindful of us as a father," he says. He thus causes him to be mindful.
There are these nine openings;
the tenth belongs to the wife.
Indeed, there are nine vital breaths in a person. || 54 ||
The navel is the tenth;
verily, he bestows the vital breaths upon the sacrificer.
Moreover, the Virāj consists of ten syllables;
the Virāj is food. By means of the Virāj, he obtains food.
The head of the sacrifice was cut off;
the gods restored it by means of the *hotrā*s. The officiating priests look on;
these indeed are the *hotrā*s.
By means of the *hotrā*s, he indeed restores the head of the sacrifice. || 55 ||
They gaze upon what is pleasing. For from what is pleasing Prajāpati created offspring; for the creation of offspring, they gaze upon what is pleasing.
From what is pleasing, indeed, Parjanya rains; Parjanya becomes one who rains abundantly;
the creatures prosper together. They look upon what is pleasing. Pleasing, indeed, is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); they become possessed of spiritual luster. || 56 ||
[5-6-12] Those who study [the Veda] look [at the sun]. They attain a full lifespan. The wife should not look [at it]. If the wife were to look, she would give birth;
however, it would consume her offspring. If she does not look, [she avoids this danger].

He would not procreate; it would consume his offspring. By reciting the *yajus* while shielding [the fire], he procreates. *Taittirīya-Āraṇyaka* – Searchable Text, Page 96 of 155 – 25.11.2005 – www.sanskritweb.net/yajurveda
It does not burn up his offspring. "May you consort with Tvaṣṭṛ," he says;
for through the consort (sappā) offspring are produced.

"The seasons indeed are the head; he pushes it forward upon all the backs, not falling down," he says; "it has gone," he says; verily for him he prepares the autumnal seasons and secures them. "Of the sages," he says; he restores the vital breaths. He causes [the sacrificer] to recite four times. 6.
[5-7-1] "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," with these words he takes up the cord for the sake of impulsion. "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says;
for the Aśvins were the two *adhvaryu* priests among the gods.
"By the two hands of Pūṣan," he says for the sake of restraint. "I take thee;

thou art Aditi’s girdle," he says for the sake of making it a sacrificial formula (yajus). "Come hither, O Iḍā! Come hither, O Aditi! Come hither, O Sarasvatī! he says. These indeed are her divine names; by means of these divine names he calls her. "So-and-so, come hither! So-and-so, come hither! So-and-so, come hither! he says. These indeed are her human names. || 58 ||
He calls her by human names; they amount to six. There are six seasons; it is by means of the seasons that he calls her.
"Thou art the turban of Aditi," he says;
this is according to the sacrificial formula itself.
"Thou art Vāyu's crest-lock," he says.
"The calf indeed has Vāyu as its deity.
'May Pūṣan release you,' he says;
for cattle have Pūṣan as their deity. || 59 ||

[5-7-3] He releases it by means of its own deity. "Cause it to be given to the Aśvins," he says. The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; through them alone he provides medicine for him. "That breast of thine which is ever-flowing," he says; thus he praises it. "O Dawn, heat! Make it warm! O Dawn, protect the heat! Make it warm for the sake of the heat! he says, just as one might say, "Give this to so-and-so."
"It is exactly so;
let Bṛhaspati attend upon you," he said. || 60 ||
Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods; by means of the Brahman, he approaches her. "Ye are the Dānavas, ye are the Peravas," he says; thus he makes them fit for sacrifice.
"He says, 'Enveloped on all sides by the red [blood],' for the sake of distinction.
'Swell for the Aśvins, swell for Sarasvatī, swell for Pūṣan, swell for Bṛhaspati,' he says;
for it swells for these very deities."
"Flow for Indra, flow for Indra," he says;
thus he gratifies Indra with his own portion.
He says "for Indra" twice. || 61 ||
[5-7-5] Therefore, Indra is the deity who receives the largest share among the gods.
With the words, "Thou art Gāyatra; thou art Traiṣṭubha; thou art Jāgata," he takes up the hoof-holders. By means of the meters, he thus takes them up.
"Come with a portion of vigor," he says;
thus he has made vigor his portion. Indeed, when the Aśvins were restoring the head of the sacrifice, they said, "Let the *vaṣaṭ* call be made for us two first."
"O Indra and Aśvins, of the honeyed *sāragha* [honey]," he says. Thus he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call for the two Aśvins first.
Moreover, he thus provides the Aśvins with their own share.

"Drink the Gharma, O Vasus, you who are worthy of sacrifice," he says. Thus he gratifies the Vasus with their own portion. If he were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, his *vaṣaṭ* call would become exhausted.
If he were not to utter *vaṣaṭ*, the *rakṣas* would destroy the sacrifice. He says *vauṣaṭ*;
thus he utters *vaṣaṭ* in a hidden manner.
His *vaṣaṭ*-call does not become stale; the *rakṣases* do not strike down his sacrifice. || 63 ||
"O Svāhā! I offer thee to the ray of the sun, the winner of rain," he says. For that which is his auspicious ray is the winner of rain.
He offers it to him alone.
"Thou art honey, the oblation," he says;
thus he makes it palatable.
"May you perform the heat of the sun," he says;
this is according to the sacrificial formula (*yajus*).
"I enclose you with heaven and earth," he says; verily, he encloses it with heaven and earth.
"By the intermediate space I take hold of you," he says; verily by the intermediate space he takes hold of him. Indeed, no human being is worthy to support him.
"By the permission of the gods and the ancestors, may I be able to support you," he says. Thus, with the permission of the gods and the ancestors, he takes it up.
Verily, they thus divide him in two.
"In that they offer in front after having first departed [from the world], he says, 'Thou art brilliance; follow after brilliance!
He thereby bestows brilliance upon him."
"Do not harm me, O one who touches heaven; do not harm me, O one who touches the intermediate space; do not harm me, O one who touches the earth," he says for the sake of non-injury.
"Thou art the sky; grant me the sky; grant me heaven; protect me from heaven," he says. He thereby invokes this very blessing.
This, indeed, is the head of the sacrifice.
The Pravargya is the self; Vāyu is the breath. He recites the names of those who raise up and those who blow away.
He restores the head of the sacrifice within himself. Without taking breath, for the continuity of the vital breaths. For five days. 66.
The sacrifice is fivefold;
as great as the sacrifice is.
He places its head [on the fire], saying:
"To Agni, accompanied by the Vasus, svāhā!
Indeed, that sun is Agni accompanied by the Vasus.
He offers it to him alone.
He says, "To Soma accompanied by Rudra, svāhā! Soma is indeed the moon, who is accompanied by Rudra;
he offers it to him alone.
"To Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas, svāhā!"—thus he says. || 67 ||
[5-7-11] Varuṇa, accompanied by the Ādityas, is indeed in the waters;
it is to him that he offers this oblation.
"To Bṛhaspati, who is accompanied by the Viśvedevas, svāhā! he says.
Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods;
it is to the Brahman that he offers him.

"To Savitṛ, the all-pervading, the far-reaching, the sovereign, the vigorous—svāhā! he says. Savitṛ is indeed the year; it is all-pervading, far-reaching, sovereign, and vigorous. To him he offers this.
"To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Fathers—svāhā! he says. Yama is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa); he is accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Fathers. || 68 ||
He offers it to him alone;
he offers it to these very deities.
They amount to ten.
The Virāj consists of ten syllables.
Food is the Virāj;
by means of the Virāj, he obtains food.
By means of the two Rauhiṇa offerings, the gods went to the heavenly world; that is why the Rauhiṇas have their name.
In that there are two *rauhiṇa* offerings, by means of these two *rauhiṇas*, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world.

"May the day, the light, rejoice with its banner; may the good light rejoice with its light, Svāhā! May the night, the light, rejoice with its banner; may the good light rejoice with its light, Svāhā!"—thus he says.
He thus supports that very Āditya in yonder world from above by means of the day and from below by means of the night;

therefore, that Āditya is supported in yonder world by day and night. "All the quarters are seated toward the south," he says;
thus he gratifies all the gods.
Thus he protects him from a defective sacrifice.

"Bring hither all the gods," he says; thereby he gratifies all the gods with their respective shares. "Drink of the honeyed gharma consecrated with Svāhā, O Aśvins," he says; thereby he gratifies the two Aśvins with their share.
"Oṃ svāhā to Agni, worthy of sacrifice; may there be well-being through the Yajus-formulas," he says. He thereby pours [the oblation] directly onto him; moreover, he has indeed made it an offering.
"O Aśvins, drink the *gharma* that gladdens the heart, with your daily aids!"—thus he says. Verily, he gratifies the two Aśvins with their own portion.
"May Heaven and Earth approve of you both"—thus he says for the sake of approval. "Svāhā to Indra! Svāhā to Indra Vaikuṇṭha!"—thus he says.
For the *puroḍāśa* is offered first to Indra.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer (*yajya*) for the *gharma*. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the oblation for the sake of driving away the *rakṣases*.
He performs the *anuyāja* for the sake of making [the offering] *svagā*-ed. "The Aśvins have drunk the *gharma*," he says. || 71 ||
[5-8-3] This has already been stated above.
He recites the response with the subsequent [verse].
"May Heaven and Earth approve of you," he says for the sake of approval.

"To that which is to be promoted, according to its form: homage to Heaven, homage to Earth," he says; this is exactly as the sacrificial formula (yajus) prescribes. "Place this sacrifice in heaven, place this sacrifice in heaven," he says; he thus causes it to go to the heavenly world.
"Go to heaven; go to the intermediate space; go to the earth," he says. He thus establishes him in these very worlds.

He establishes it in the very quarters. He says, "Go to the gods who drink the Gharma; go to the fathers who drink the Gharma"; he thus establishes it in both.
When it overflows—

therefore, it is auspicious when swelling.
When it swells toward the east...
That which belongs to the gods is [the northern fire];

that which is directed northward [belongs to the gods].
That belongs to the Rudras. He causes it to swell toward the east and the north; he has performed [the rite] among the gods.
Now, moreover, he causes it to swell toward all the quarters; all the quarters prosper. He causes it to swell within the enclosing sticks.
"For the non-falling away of splendor;
swell for food, swell for strength," he says.
He bestows nourishment and vigor upon the sacrificer.
"Swell for the sacrificer," he says;
thus he invokes this blessing for the sacrificer himself.
"Make me swell for preeminence," he says;
thus he invokes this blessing for himself.
"For brilliance thee, for splendor thee, for power thee, for prosperity thee," he says.
Just as it is with the Yajus formula, so it is here:

He establishes him in Brahman itself;

"To Pūṣan’s seed, svāhā! he says.

He should not look back.
Whatever he should investigate. || 78 ||
His eye would become impaired;

"Carry me across from day to night; protect me! This is your fuel-stick, O Agni; with it may you be kindled; grant me life; do not deprive me of splendor," he says.
Verily, he bestows life and splendor upon him.
"Carry me across from night to day; protect me! This is your fuel-stick, O Agni; with it may you be kindled; grant me life; do not deprive me of splendor," he says.
Verily, he bestows life and luster upon him.
"Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!"—thus he says.

"Sustain [the heat]," he says; thus he offers it to those very ones who drink the *gharma* of speech. He should look upon it [thinking], "Is it to be offered? "In the fire," he says; thus they bestow and protect it. (Eight and seven. 8.

[[5-9-1]] He offers three oblations with the formula, "O Gharma, that heat of yours which is in heaven... By means of the meters, he thus expiates his heat from these worlds. First he offers at this distance; then at this distance; then at this distance.
There are these three worlds.
From these very worlds he expiates his impurity. "May Anumati favor us today," he says for the sake of Anumati. "Thee for the protection from heaven," he says.
"By day he has supported these worlds; for the protection against the Supreme Brahman, I take you," he says. || 83 ||

[5-9-2] He has thus supported offspring within these very worlds. "For the protection of breath," he says; verily, he has established the vital breaths within the offspring. The Pravargya is indeed the head of the sacrifice.
Now, that Pravargya is truly the sun.
If he were to set it down facing south, west, or north, he would strike the head of the sacrifice askew. He sets it down facing east;
thus he restores the head of the sacrifice from the very front.
He carries it out toward the east;

therefore, yonder sun rises in the east. They carry along [the implements]: the hoof-shaped receptacles, the fans, and the fire-stirring sticks. Thus he makes it possessed of its own self and possessed of its body; he becomes possessed of his own self in yonder world.
Whoever knows thus:
they are made of Udumbara wood;
the Udumbara is indeed strength (ūrg).
Verily, he wins nourishment;
for he has followed along the path. 85.

[5-9-4] The *rakṣases* seek to destroy the sacrifice. The *prastotṛ* follows it with the *sāman*. The *sāman* is indeed the slayer of *rakṣases*; it serves for the driving away of the *rakṣases*. He approaches the finale (*nidhana*) three times.
These are the three worlds.
From these very worlds he drives away the *rakṣases*. Each person approaches the *nidhana*; for each person is possessed by *rakṣases*. It is for the purpose of driving away the *rakṣases*. 86.
If one were to set it down upon the earth, he would afflict the earth with pain.
*Taittirīya-Āraṇyaka* (Searchable Text), Page 104 of 155, 25.11.2005, www.sanskritweb.net/yajurveda

If [he were to set it down] in water, he would afflict the waters with impurity. If in plants, he would afflict the plants with impurity. If in trees, he would afflict the trees with impurity. He sets it out after placing gold [beneath it]; for gold is indeed immortality.
[5-9-6] He establishes him in immortality. "Thou art auspicious, a bestower of well-being," he says three times while pouring around [the fire]. For Agni is threefold.
It is exactly as much as the fire itself; he thus pacifies its heat. He goes around it three times again.
There are six [fingers];
there are six seasons.
Verily, by means of the seasons he pacifies his heat. "The navel of Order has four corners," he says. || 88 ||
This earth, indeed, is the *ṛta*;
this very [fire] is its navel.
Because of the Pravargya rite, he speaks thus:
"The Sadas is all-sustaining," he says.

"May he be free from hatred, free from crookedness," he says, for the purpose of driving away the enemy. "O Gharma, this is your food, this is your nourishment," with these words he fills [the vessel] with curds mixed with honey. Curds are indeed strength and the means of eating;
verily, he endows him with strength and the means of eating. || 89 ||
He becomes one who does not hunger,
he who knows thus.
"You are Ranti, the divine Gandharva," he says. He thus proclaims his form, his greatness, his delight, and his kinship. "May I be united with life, united with breath," he says;
he thereby invokes this very blessing. "May that one who hates us and whom we hate be separated," he says; this is indeed a spell against him.
"He has bellowed, the tawny bull," he says;
for he is indeed a bull. 90.
"The tawny bull is great like Mitra, beautiful to behold," he says.
The *Taittirīya-Āraṇyaka*—Searchable Text, page 105 of 155—25.11.2005—www.sanskritweb.net/yajurveda: "He thus praises him [the sacrificer] with this [verse]:
'Thou art consciousness, thy womb is the ocean,' he says."
He causes him to go to his very own womb.

He says, "Homage be to you; do not harm me," for the sake of non-injury. He says, "Viśvāvasu, the Gandharva of Soma. Whatever of this [Soma] they cause to disappear while it is being prepared, that he thereby replenishes for him.
He says, "May Viśvāvasu sing this to us. (91)
This has already been stated previously.
He recites the response with the subsequent [verse].
"May he, impelling our thoughts, protect our thoughts," he says; thus he prepares the seasons for him.
"The Gandharva has proclaimed their immortals," he says;
the vital breaths, indeed, are the immortals.
He prepares the very vital breaths for him. "O divine Gharma, as a god you have approached the gods," he says; for he is indeed a god and approaches the gods.
"I here, a human, [approach] humans," he says. || 92 ||
For this one, being a human, approaches other humans.
When the Lord is about to remove the Pravargya vessel, he says:
"Do not remove [the fire] after [leaving behind] offspring and cattle; do not exclude me from the drinking of Soma!
Go forth together with offspring, together with the increase of wealth!"
He bestows offspring, cattle, and the drinking of Soma upon himself.
"May the waters and plants be friendly to us," he says;
he thereby invokes this very blessing.
"May those who hate us and whom we hate have evil friends," he says; this is indeed his incantation. Verily, he falls away from this world.
He who puts away the Pravargya ritual returns and offers oblations on the Gārhapatya fire with two verses addressed to the Sun, beginning with "udu tyam" and "citram.
This Gārhapatya fire is indeed this world.
He becomes firmly established in this very world.
For that sun is indeed the heavenly world;
therefore, the two verses belong to Sūrya.
By that very [act], he does not go from the heavenly world. || 93 ||

"May Brahmā protect you from the beyond," he says; he places [the gold] along [the cord] for the warding off of the Rākṣasas. "Gold indeed drives away the Rākṣasas," they say, for it is this [gold] that overcomes them. "May he sing [of us]," he says; he says this regarding men. This [section] consists of eight [verses]. 9.
The gods milked Prajāpati for the bright milk; it did not suffice for them. Agni then distributed it.
Those became the Śukriya Sāmans.
From them, their essence flowed forth.

These became the Śukra-yajus formulas; these are indeed the "Śukriyas" of the Śukriya hymns. Of these two, one is the milk of the Sāman, and the other is the milk of the gods—that which is the milk of the cow.
That is the milk of the *sāman*;
it is the milk of the she-goat.
That is the milk of the gods; therefore, whenever they proceed with these sacrificial formulas (yajus), they proceed with milk.

Thus, they satisfy Prajāpati and the gods with milk and food. He indeed partakes directly of the Pravargya for whom the Pravargya is performed by one who knows thus. One should remove it onto the high altar (uttaravedī) for one who desires splendor.
Or rather, the high altar is brilliance. || 95 ||
The Pravargya is splendor.
By means of splendor itself, he causes splendor to prosper. One who desires food should remove it upon the high altar (uttaravedi).
The Pravargya is indeed the head of the sacrifice;
the Uttaravedi is the mouth.
He joins the face with the head for the sake of eating food; he indeed becomes an eater of food.
Wherever birds settle around this [fire] when it has been moved out, around those people the birds will settle during that year. || 96 ||

Therefore, one should set it down on the high altar (uttaravedi) for the protection of offspring. Or one may set it down either in front or behind; for this light rises in the east and sets in the west.
He causes it to be taken out according to its own source. He should take it out in the midst of the waters;
for this light was born from the midst of the waters, and the Pravargya is light. Thus he establishes it in its own source. || 97 ||
[5-10-5] Against whom one may feel enmity;
wherever that person may be.
One should remove [the vessel] in that direction. This indeed is Agni Vaiśvānara;
for the Pravargya is he.
Verily, he sets him in motion with Agni Vaiśvānara. He should set it down on a branch of the Udumbara tree;
the Udumbara is strength, and breath is food.
Śuggharmaḥ || 98 ||
"Here, with this grief of such-and-such a person, son of such-and-such a lineage, I burn away his breath," he says. Verily, by means of that very grief, he burns away his breath;
he swiftly meets with distress.
Where the *darbha* grasses are continuous with their tips pointing downward,
there he should remove [the fire] for one who desires rain;
these indeed are the waters named "Unexhausting."
As for the darbha grass:
that sun indeed sends rain down from here;
that very sun bestows rain upon him.
Those waters flow forth, restrained by the desert. || 99 ||
The milk of the cow is the high altar; they sit down and establish it; they proceed with the Gharma oblation. || 10 ||
Prajāpati was being gathered together; he is the sovereign (saṃrāj) once gathered. The Gharma has been set forth; the Mahāvīra vessel has been placed on the fire.
This Pravargya, indeed, is yonder sun.
He gave these names; whoever knows thus, they know him by name. So say the exponents of Brahman. 100.
He who addresses a superior person by his name indeed brings him misfortune; he brings misfortune upon himself, and they bring misfortune upon him who knows thus.
Therefore, knowing this, one should call it "Gharma" by day and "Samrāj" by night.
These two indeed are its beloved bodies; these two are its beloved names. Verily, he [unites] with it through its own beloved body.
He causes [the sacrificer] to prosper with a beloved name;
his fame goes before him as he approaches the assembly from afar. Gāyatrī departed from the gods.
The gods attained her by means of the *pravargya* rite; they obtained her by means of the *pravargya*. In that he performs the *pravargya* twenty-four times, he thereby attains the *gāyatrī* metre.
He obtains the Gāyatrī;
his fame spreads from the very beginning of his people; he is established as belonging to the Viśvedevas. || 102 ||

The Vasu-cup belongs to the Vasus when [the Soma] has been poured out; the Soma-cup belongs to Soma when it is being scattered; the cup for the Aśvins belongs to the Aśvins when the curd-mixture is being brought forward; the cup for the Maruts belongs to the Maruts while it is boiling; the cup for Pūṣan belongs to Pūṣan when it has reached the end [of the cooking].
The Sarasvatī is flowing; the arrow is grasped by Mitra;
the wind is rising with brilliance; Prajāpati is being carried away; Vāk is being offered as an oblation. || 103 ||
[5-11-5] This Pravargya, indeed, is truly that sun; he assumed these names. He who knows thus [attains them].
"Vidura by name," so say those who discourse on Brahman. "Since that which is made of clay does not partake of the oblation, why then does this [clay Vidura] partake of it?
One should reply: "This is Speech."
He places speech within speech itself. || 104 ||
Therefore, he attains [it].
This Prajāpati, indeed, is divided twelvefold.
By that which is the Pravargya,
and by that which precedes the Avakāśas,
he created progeny.
By means of the spaces, he created the gods and asuras;
that which was above the spaces,
by that he created food.
Food is Prajāpati;
indeed, he is Prajāpati. || 105 ||
They say that when he is seated in the body or when he is being offered oblations, this one, as the Speech-offering, bestows [the fruit]. || 11 ||
Having become Savitṛ, he is initiated on the first day; through that, he attains his desires. *Taittirīya-Āraṇyaka* — Searchable Text, Page 109 of 155 — 25.11.2005 — www.sanskritweb.net/yajurveda

When he is initiated on the second day, having become Agni, he goes to the gods. When he is initiated on the third day, having become Vāyu, he goes to the vital breaths. When he is initiated on the fourth day...
Having become the sun, he goes forth with his rays; when [the fire] is carried forward on the fifth day, having become the moon, he goes forth with the stars. || 106 ||

When he is consecrated on the sixth day, having become the Season (*ṛtu*), he goes to the *saṃvatsara* (the year). When he is consecrated on the seventh day, having become Dhātṛ, he goes to the *śakvarī* (verse). When he is consecrated on the eighth day, having become Bṛhaspati, he goes to the *gāyatrī* (verse). When he is consecrated on the ninth day...
Having become Mitra, he goes to these three worlds; when he is initiated on the tenth day, having become Varuṇa, he goes to the Virāj.
When he is consecrated on the eleventh day, having become Indra, he attains the Triṣṭubh meter. When he is consecrated on the twelfth day...

Becoming Soma, he goes to the pressing. Because [the fire] is carried forward before the Upasads, therefore it goes from here toward those worlds beyond, burning. Because it is carried forward after the Upasads, therefore it comes from those worlds beyond toward these worlds, burning. He who knows thus indeed burns. 108.
Having gone to the constellations, he goes to the Virāj and shines. || 12 ||

The gods indeed performed the Sattra of Savitṛ. "In an enclosed space, O Brahman, we shall proceed with the rite. "Agni is your head; the neck of the god [is yours]; the halter is for all the quarters, O Gharma. That which is your offspring, O Prajāpati; Prajāpati being gathered together, having become Savitṛ, [there are] twelve. (12)

The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session (*satra*). This *khadira* tree was [prepared] in an enclosed space (*pariśrita*) in successive order; furthermore, it is for the sake of warding off the *rakṣases*. Verily, the Aśvins are the Brahman among the gods; drink the *gharma*! Verily, the tawny bull is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). As for him who is more wealthy—according to their names—one hundred and eight [verses]. 108.
May it be auspicious for us; may it not abandon us. Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
I sprinkle you with the sacrificial formula for progeny, long life, and wealth.
Taittirīya Āraṇyaka – Searchable Text, Page 110 of 155 – 25.11.2005 – www.sanskritweb.net/yajurveda | Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ.

[6-1-1] Departing along the great slopes, you have spied out the path for many. Pay honor with an oblation to Yama, the son of Vivasvat, the king and gatherer of men. This garment has first come to you; it fell down here when you wore it in the past. Look back upon your sacrifices and pious works, and the sacrificial fee given by you in various ways among your kinsmen. I yoke these two carriers for you, for the journey to the world of the living, so that by them you may go to the abode of Yama and to those who have performed good deeds.

May Pūṣan, the wise one, the guardian of the world whose cattle are never lost, drive you forth from here. May he entrust you to these ancestors, and may Agni deliver you to the well-disposed gods. Pūṣan knows all these quarters; may he lead us by the path most free from fear. Bestowing well-being, glowing, accompanied by a full host of heroes, may he, the wise one, go before us without negligence. 1.

[6-1-2] May Āyus, the all-encompassing life-force, protect you; may Pūṣan protect you on the distant path ahead. Where the doers of good deeds dwell, where they have gone—there may the divine Savitṛ establish you. O Lord of the World, this is the oblation for Agni, the possessor of wealth: Svāhā!
O long-lived one, we wipe away the stains upon the man,
so that here no other shall come before us until old age. O long-lived one, I have released your breath.
With your body come to the earth by your own power; with your progeny, bring us here, O Mother.
Do not grieve, for I am your beloved, a goddess remaining true even as you depart for the world of the fathers.
O you who possess all boons, clothing yourself in the sky, shower both our worlds with your milk.

[6-1-3] This woman, choosing the world of her husband, lies down beside you, O mortal who has passed away. Protecting all that is ancient, bestow upon her offspring and wealth here. Rise up, O woman, toward the world of the living; come to this one whose life has departed. You have entered into this state of wifehood for your husband, the one who took your hand and wooed you. Taking the gold from the hand of the dead man, [I take it] for his prosperity, for sacred knowledge, for splendor, and for strength.

Right here, may you and we be well-disposed; may we conquer all rivals and adversaries. Taking from the hand of the deceased the bow—for the sake of glory, for dominion, for vigor, and for strength—right here, may you and we be well-disposed; may we conquer all rivals and adversaries. Taking from the hand of the deceased the amulet—for the sake of glory, for the prosperity of the people, and for strength—right here, may you and we be well-disposed; may we conquer all rivals and adversaries. (3)

[6-1-4] O Agni, do not overturn this cup; it is dear to the gods and to those worthy of Soma. This is the cup from which the gods drink; in it, let the immortal gods rejoice. Envelop yourself with the cow-hides as Agni’s armor; cover yourself completely with fat and marrow. Let not the bold one, exulting in his heat and desiring to consume you, seize you by twisting you around. Do not burn him up, O Agni; do not scorch him; do not strip away his skin nor his body.
When you have cooked him, O Jātavedas, then send him forth to the Fathers.
When you have cooked him, O Jātavedas, then deliver him to the Fathers.
When he goes toward this path of the departed, then let him become subject to the will of the gods.
Let your eye go to the sun, your breath to the wind; go to heaven and to earth according to your inherent nature.

Go to the waters, if it is there that your welfare lies; take your stand among the plants with your bodies. The goat has no share [in the sacrifice]; burn him with heat, let your flame burn him, let your radiance burn him.
O Jātavedas, with those forms of yours that are auspicious, carry me to where the worlds of the righteous are.
Truly, you are this; from me, you are that. Truly, you are his source.

O Vaiśvānara, son, maker of the world for your father, O Jātavedas, carry us to where the worlds of the righteous are. (4) Knowing, turn back toward us; may we conquer our adversaries with our bodies. (1) [Total: 5]

To those who are the guardians of this path, svāhā! To those who are the protectors of this path, svāhā! To those who are the defenders of this path, svāhā! To the announcer, svāhā! To the one who does not announce, svāhā! To the one who praises, svāhā! To the one who reviles, svāhā! To Agni, the performer of rites, svāhā! To him whom we do not know here, svāhā! He who, sweating, brings fuel for thee, or heats his head out of devotion to thee—

From every part of heaven, O giver of wealth, grant us protection; for you were born from him, and from you may he be born again. To Agni Vaiśvānara, for the heavenly world, Svāhā! (5) Those five [verses] of his are from you. (2)
With his lofty banner Agni shines; the Bull bellows aloud, making all things manifest. From the very ends of heaven he has come down to me; the Buffalo has grown great in the lap of the waters.
This is one light for you, and beyond that is another; enter into union with the third light. Be gracious to our body when we rest; be dear to the gods in the highest dwelling-place.

When they behold you with longing in their hearts as you fly like a bird of prey toward the vault of heaven—the golden-winged messenger of Varuṇa, the restless bird in the abode of Yama—run past the two dogs, the sons of Saramā, the four-eyed brindled ones, by the straight path.

Then go to the benevolent fathers who rejoice in revelry together with Yama. O King Yama, entrust him to those two dogs of yours, the guardians, four-eyed, watching over the paths, beholding men; grant him well-being and freedom from disease.

[6-3-2] The two messengers of Yama, Uruṇasā and Ulumbala, who satisfy themselves with food, roam about among those who are powerless. May they restore to us today here the life-force so that we may behold the sun; may it be auspicious for us. For some, Soma purifies itself; others attend to the clarified butter. To those for whom the honey flows forth—may he go even to them.
May he go even to those who fight in the great battles, the heroes who cast away their bodies,
or those who give thousands as sacrificial fees;
to those who are invincible through austerity and who have attained heaven by austerity.

May those who have performed great austerities go even to the gods. O wealthy ones, cross over the stony river; be joyful, arise, and advance together, O friends! Here we leave behind those who were unkind; may we overcome auspicious strengths.
That which is indeed the filter of the god Savitṛ, spread with a thousand streams across the mid-air—by which he purified Indra from affliction—I purify myself, my entire body, with that.

Those branches which fall away from the kingdom, struck down while seeking a king—O Dhātṛ, may all those be purified by this cleansing; unite us with progeny, wealth, and splendor. Rising above the darkness, we behold the higher light.

We have gone to the god Sūrya among the gods, the highest light. May Dhātṛ purify me; may Savitṛ purify me with the splendor of Agni and the luster of Sūrya. (8) Bestow [this] upon me. These eight [verses] follow. (3)
That fire which we have churned for you, as one churns for a bull to cook its food— that very fire we now appease for you with milk and with water.
O Agni, that which you have completely consumed, that do you extinguish again.

May the *kyaṃbūra*, the *pāka*, the *dūrvā*, and the *vālaka* grow here. O cool one, O you who possess coolness, O refreshing one, O you who possess refreshment! With the *maṇḍūkī*, well-united, appease my internal heat; bring peace to my fire. May the waters from the desert be peaceful for you; may the waters from the springs be peaceful for you. May the waters of the ocean be peaceful for you; may the waters of the rain be peaceful for you. May the flowing streams be peaceful for your body; may the waters of the wells be peaceful for you. May the mist rain down peacefully upon you; may the dew fall peacefully upon you. 9.
[6-4-2] Release him again, O Agni, to the fathers—he who, offered to you, moves with the *svadhā* offerings.
Wearing a long life, let him approach his remnant; let him be united with a body, O Jātavedas.

Unite with the fathers, with the *svadhā* offerings, and with the merit of your sacrifices and good works in the highest heaven. Go to that place which you choose upon the earth; there may the god Savitṛ establish you.

Whatever the black bird has pecked at you, the ant, the serpent, or even the wild beast—may Agni and Soma, who has entered into the Brāhmaṇa, make all that free from debt for you. Arise, O body, gather yourself together! Do not abandon this limb, do not cast off this frame.
Go to that place which you choose upon the earth; there may the god Savitṛ establish you.
This is one for you; beyond this is another for you. Unite with the third light. Be gracious to our body when entering [the fire], dear to the gods in the highest dwelling place.
Arise, go forth, run forward, and make a home for yourself in the highest heaven.
In harmony with Yama and Yamī, ascend this highest firmament.

The stone-bearing, wealthy [waters], which are indeed the purifier of the god Savitṛ; those which have fallen from the kingdom—may Dhātṛ purify us from them, as we rise up out of the darkness. You are born from this; may he be born from you.
To Agni Vaiśvānara, for the heavenly world, svāhā! 10.
There are five [syllables] in the *avaśīyat* [meter] at the place of assembly. || 4 ||

[6-5-1] May Yama come here with his gracious favors and well-directed protections; may he sit upon this well-spread sacred grass for my strength, for my progeny, and for the slaying of my enemies. When you two came together like twins striving in unison, the god-seeking men brought you forward. Sit down in your own place, you who know it; be seated comfortably for our Soma-juice. Press the Soma for Yama; offer the oblation to Yama.
To Yama indeed goes the sacrifice, with Agni as its well-prepared messenger.
Offer oblations rich in ghee to Yama and step forward;
may he secure for us among the gods a long life that we may live it out.
Offer to King Yama the most honey-sweet oblation.
Homage to these seers, the ancestors of old, who were the first makers of the path. || 11 ||

[6-5-2] He who alone is the ruler of this earthly world, the vast expanse; sing of Yama, whose fame is widespread, the king who cannot be resisted. Sing of Yama, whose fame is widespread, the king who cannot be resisted. By whom the waters, the rivers, and the deserts [were established], by whom the sky and the earth were made firm—King Yama presides over the gift of horses that have golden girths, are well-yoked, have golden eyes, and hooves like iron, which never fail.

Yama has supported the earth; Yama has supported this entire world. To Yama belongs all that exists within Mitra, and that which breathes, protected by Vāyu. As there are five, as there are six, and as there are fifteen seers—whosoever knows Yama, let him speak, for he alone is a seer who truly understands.

[6-5-3] He flies with the *trikadrukas*; the six wide ones; this one alone is the Great One. The *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, and all the meters—these are all established in Yama. Day after day, leading away cattle, horses, men, and the moving world, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is not yet satisfied with the five tribes of men. Under King Yama, the son of Vivasvat, those people are separated out:
both those who here desire the truth and those who are speakers of untruth.

O King, they are distinguished here; then they approach you—those gods whom men revere and those brahmins whom they honor. Upon that tree with beautiful foliage where Yama drinks together with the gods, there our Father, the Lord of the People, listens to the ancient songs. To those who know the makers of paths, he listens. 5. 13.

[6-6-1] I offer this oblation into Vaiśvānara, this thousandfold fountain with a hundred streams. In him, while he swells, may he support our father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. The drop has fallen along the earth, along the sky, along this womb and that which was before. I offer the drop as it moves through the third womb, following the seven officiating priests. This ocean, a hundred-streamed fountain, expanding in the midst of the world—milking ghee for humanity from Aditi, O Agni, do not harm us in the highest heaven.

Depart, go away, and creep away from here—those who are here, both ancient and recent. May Yama, manifest through days, waters, and nights, grant him a dwelling place. Savitṛ has placed these bodies in the lap of Mother Earth; let the sacrificial fires be joined with them. 14.
Prosperity to the draft-animals, prosperity to the men; may the ploughshare plow with prosperity.
May the leather thongs be fastened with prosperity; raise the goad with prosperity. O Śuna and Sīra, bestow prosperity upon us!
O Śuna and Sīra, with that milk which you created in heaven, sprinkle this [earth] here.
O Sītā, we revere you; be favorable to us, O auspicious one.
As the moon is not lost, as the moon is not fruitless,
so do I place these bodies upon the lap of the mother earth; through them, O Aditi,
be auspicious.
Be released, O inviolable ones, paths leading to the gods; we have crossed over to the further shore of this darkness.
We have attained the light; we have gone to the sun. 15.

[6-6-3] The winds blow forth, the lightnings fly; the plants shoot up, and heaven overflows. Nourishment is born for every living being when Parjanya protects the earth with his seed. Just as the five tribes of men sowed a home for Yama, so do I sow this home, that we may be many in the world of the living.
O you who are piled up, well-heaped, and piled upwards, take your place; O Fathers, you are the deities. May Prajāpati establish you; through that deity [may it be so]. "Swell up!
Let your [milk] gather together! (16)
We have come to the inviolable ones, seven and [one]. 6.

[6-7-1] I lift up the earth; I place this world around me, free from harm. May the fathers support this pillar for you; may Yama establish your dwelling here. We offer this sacred grass to the fathers; while living, we shall offer what is higher to the gods. Ascend that [grass], become fit for sacrifice; in harmony with Yama and Yamī, do thou ascend. Let not the two trees press upon thee, nor thou, O Earth, thy mother.
For here thou shalt go to the fathers, to find fuel in the realm of Yama.
Let not the two trees oppress thee, nor the great Earth, thy mother.

Savitṛ has placed these bodies in the lap of the mother Earth;

To you who have eyes and hear, I speak: do not harm our progeny, nor our heroes. May the wind be auspicious for you, may the sun’s heat be auspicious for you, and may the plants be auspicious for you. May the quarters of space be favorable and gracious to me.
I set you down in the world of earth; you are the protection for such-and-such a person. The Pitṛs are the deity.

I settle you upon the back of the atmosphere, you upon the sky, you upon the quarters, you upon the ridge of the firmament, you upon the summit of the sun; you are the protection of so-and-so. The Pitṛs are the deity.

The ten-syllabled [meter]—protect it, guard it, I entrust it to you; may the Pitṛs and the deities not harm you therein. May Prajāpati settle you with that deity. Fill the world; may those [waters] yield milk for him.

Spreading [the sacrifice], may they bring peace; svāhā! May the students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) come from all sides; svāhā! To Dhātṛ, svāhā! And one. 4.

That is Brahman;
that is the Self;

"Suva" is in the sun;

[7-7-1] Earth, the intermediate space, heaven, the quarters, and the intermediate directions; fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the stars; water, herbs, trees, space, and the self—this is with reference to the objective world (adhibhūta). Now, with reference to the self (adhyātma):

The out-breath (*prāṇa*), the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the in-breath (*apāna*), the upward-breath (*udāna*), and the level-breath (*samāna*); the eye, the ear, the mind, speech, and the skin; the skin, the flesh, the sinews, the bone, and the marrow—having laid this out in detail, the Seer said: "All this is indeed fivefold (*pāṅkta*). "Om" is Brahman;

[7-9-1] Righteousness (*ṛta*) and the study and teaching of the Veda; truth (*satya*) and the study and teaching of the Veda; austerity (*tapas*) and the study and teaching of the Veda; self-control (*dama*) and the study and teaching of the Veda; tranquility (*śama*) and the study and teaching of the Veda; the sacred fires (*agni*) and the study and teaching of the Veda; the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*) and the study and teaching of the Veda; guests (*atithi*) and the study and teaching of the Veda; human duties (*mānuṣa*) and the study and teaching of the Veda; and progeny (*prajā*) and the study and teaching of the Veda.

And offspring, as well as study and teaching of the Veda; these are the six.
I am the shaker of the tree;
my fame is like the ridge of a mountain.

Thus [ends] the sixth [section]. 10.
[7-11-1] Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the pupil: "Speak the truth.

Do not neglect your private study of the Veda.

those Brahmins who are more excellent and more venerable than we are.

as they would conduct themselves toward them, so should you conduct yourself toward them— this is the instruction.

this is the secret doctrine of the Veda;
this is the teaching.

The Lord of the universe, the inner ruler, eternal, auspicious, and infallible; Nārāyaṇa, the great object of knowledge, the soul of the universe, the supreme refuge; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light, the Self, Nārāyaṇa is supreme; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman-reality, Nārāyaṇa is supreme; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditator, Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditation; whatever exists in this entire world, whether it is seen or even heard—[all that is Nārāyaṇa]. Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without—endless, undecaying, the seer, the end of the ocean, the source of bliss for the universe. The heart, resembling the interior of a lotus bud, faces downward;

Continuous with the veins, it hangs like a hollow bud;
at its end is a subtle aperture, within which everything is established.

In its center stands the great fire, with universal radiance and faces on every side. That ageless sage, consuming the food as it arrives, remains dividing it; his rays extend continuously upward, downward, and across.

In the center of that [body], a flame of fire is situated, extremely subtle and directed upwards. It is as radiant as a streak of lightning in the midst of dark blue clouds; it is slender like the awn of a grain of wild rice (nīvāra), yellow, brilliant, and minute. In the center of that flame, the Supreme Self (paramātman) is situated.
He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Hari, he is Indra; he is the imperishable, supreme, self-ruling Lord. Or rather, there are six [names] in continuous succession. 13.30–31.

Truth is supreme; truth is the highest. By truth the virtuous never fall from the heavenly world, for truth belongs to the good; therefore, they delight in truth. Penance—there is no penance higher than fasting; for that which is the highest penance is invincible and unassailable; therefore, they delight in penance. Self-restraint—the student of sacred knowledge is ever restrained; therefore, they delight in self-restraint. Tranquility—the sages in the forest possess tranquility; therefore, they delight in tranquility. Charity—all beings praise charity; there is nothing more difficult to practice than charity.

Therefore, they delight in giving, [thinking] "this is dharma"; for by dharma all this is encompassed, and there is nothing more difficult than dharma; therefore, they delight in dharma. They say, "procreation"—because it is most abundant, offspring are born most abundantly; therefore, most people delight in procreation. He says, "the sacred fires"—therefore, the sacred fires should be established. He says, "the Agnihotra"—therefore, they delight in the Agnihotra. He says, "sacrifice"—for the gods are sacrifice; therefore, they delight in sacrifice. He says, "the mental [sacrifice]"—therefore, it is the wise alone who [delight in it].

They delight in the mind; renunciation is Brahman. Brahman is indeed supreme, for Brahman is the highest. These other things are indeed inferior; renunciation alone surpasses them all. He who knows this—this is the Upanishad. 99. 78.

[10-79-1] Hāruṇi Suparṇeya, the son of Prajāpati, approached his father Prajāpati and asked, "What do the venerable ones declare to be the supreme? To him he replied: "By truth the wind blows; by truth the sun shines in the sky.
(Taittirīya Āraṇyaka)

Truth is the foundation of speech; everything is established in truth. Therefore, they say truth is supreme. By austerity, the gods first attained godhood; by austerity, the seers found the heavenly world. By austerity, we shall drive away our rivals and enemies. Everything is established in austerity; therefore, they say austerity is supreme. By self-control, the self-controlled shake off evil; by self-control, the students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins) went to the heavenly world. Self-control is invincible among living beings; everything is established in self-control. Therefore, self-control is supreme.

The tranquil ones say that tranquility is supreme; through tranquility they practice auspiciousness, and by tranquility the sages attained heaven. Tranquility is invincible among beings; everything is established in tranquility. Therefore, they say that tranquility is supreme. Sacrificial fee is the protection of sacrifices; in this world, all beings depend upon the giver. By giving, they drove away enemies; by giving, those who hate become friends. Everything is established in giving; therefore, they say that giving is supreme. Righteousness is the foundation of the universe.

In this world, the foundation of the universe is dharma; people approach the most righteous man with dharma; by means of dharma one drives away evil; everything is established in dharma; therefore they say that dharma is supreme. Procreation indeed is the foundation in this world; he who skillfully extends the thread of his offspring becomes free from debt to the ancestors; that alone is his freedom from debt; therefore they say that procreation is supreme. The three fires are indeed the triple Veda, the path leading to the gods: the Gārhapatya fire is the *Ṛgveda* and the earth.

The *Rathantara* is the Anvāhāryapacana fire; the Yajus is the intermediate space; the *Vāmadevya* is the Āhavanīya fire; the Sāman is the heavenly world; and the *Bṛhat* is [the firmament]. Therefore, they call the fires the supreme. The Agnihotra is the atonement for the household; it is well-sacrificed, well-offered, and the entrance to the sacrificial rites. It is the light of the heavenly world; therefore, they call the Agnihotra the supreme. "Sacrifice" (yajña)—for by sacrifice the gods went to heaven; by sacrifice they drove away the Asuras; by sacrifice enemies become friends; [it is] in sacrifice.

Everything is established in that; therefore, they call the sacrifice supreme. It is indeed mental, belonging to Prajāpati, and is a means of purification. With the mind as his instrument, one sees what is good through the mental sacrifice. Through the mental sacrifice, the seers created all beings; everything is established in the mental sacrifice; therefore, they call the mental sacrifice supreme. The wise say that renunciation (*nyāsa*) is Brahman. What is Brahman? He is the All (*viśva*). Who is he? He is the Self-existent (*svayaṃbhu*). Who is Prajāpati? He is the Year (*saṃvatsara*). This year is yonder Āditya (the Sun). That Person who is in the Sun is Parameṣṭhin.

Brahman is the Self. By those rays wherewith the sun shines, Parjanya rains; by Parjanya, herbs and trees are produced; by herbs and trees, food comes into being; by food, the vital breaths; by the vital breaths, strength; by strength, austerity; by austerity, faith; by faith, the intellect; by the intellect, discernment; by discernment, the mind; by the mind, peace; by peace, the heart; by the heart, memory; by memory, recognition; by recognition, knowledge; by knowledge, one causes the Self to be known. Therefore, [it is called] *anna* (food).

Giving all these, he gives from food; from food the vital breaths of beings arise, from the vital breaths the mind, from the mind discernment, and from discernment bliss—Brahman, the source. This very Puruṣa is fivefold, having a fivefold nature, by whom all this is woven together—the earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the quarters, and the intermediate directions. He indeed is this entire world; he is the past, he is the future; he is fashioned by the seeker of knowledge, born of Truth, established in wealth, faith, truth, and majesty, the most excellent of ascetic heat. Having known him...

Knowing this, do not approach death again with such thoughts in mind or heart; therefore, they say that renunciation (*nyāsa*) is superior to these austerities (*tapas*). "O Vasu, O Raṇva, you are all-pervading; you are the uniter in breath; you are Brahman, the sustainer of the universe; you are the giver of splendor; you are Agni; you are the giver of luster; you are the giver of glory to the sun; you are the giver of radiance to the moon. You are taken with a support (*upayāma*); I take you for the sake of the Great Brahman. Om!—thus one should yoke the Self. This indeed is the Great Upaniṣad, the secret of the gods. He who knows this [attains] Brahman.
He attains greatness; therefore, "the greatness of Brahman"—this is the Upaniṣad. || 100 || || 79 ||

For one who knows this, the sacrifice is as follows: the self is the sacrificer; faith is the wife; the body is the fuel; the chest is the altar; the hair is the sacrificial grass; the Veda is the tuft; the heart is the sacrificial post; desire is the clarified butter; anger is the victim; austerity is the fire; self-restraint is the pacifier; the sacrificial fee is speech; the Hotṛ priest is the out-breath; the Udgātṛ priest is the in-breath; the Adhvaryu priest is the sight; the Brahman priest is the mind; the Āgnīdhra priest is the hearing. As long as he is consecrated, that is his initiation; what he eats is the oblation; what he drinks is his drinking of Soma; and what he enjoys is the Upasad rites.
As he moves about, sits down, and stands up, that is the Pravargya; his mouth is the Āhavanīya fire.

The *vyāhṛtis* are his oblations; that which is his consciousness, he offers as the sacrifice. That which he eats in the evening and in the morning is the fuel-stick (*samidh*). The morning, midday, and evening meals are the *savana*s (pressings). Day and night are the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. The half-months and months are the *cāturmāsya*s. The seasons are the *paśubandha*s. The years and the *parivatsara*s are the *ahargaṇa*s. This entire life is indeed a *sattra* (long sacrificial session); death is its final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). This is the *agnihotra* and *sattra* that lasts until old age and death.

One who knows this and dies during the northern course of the sun, having attained the majesty of the gods, goes to union with the Sun. But he who dies during the southern course, having attained the majesty of the ancestors, reaches union with and the same world as the Moon. A Brahmin who knows this conquers these two majesties of the Sun and the Moon; therefore, he attains the majesty of Brahman. "Therefore, he attains the majesty of Brahman"—this is the Upanishad. 101. 80.

Of that which was done by the gods, eleven [parts]; O gods, whatever desire you have performed, whatever anger you have performed—two by two, I offer sesame seeds into the fire. Forty-one; that Brahman, nine; established in faith and in breath, I offer the immortal.

Twenty-four [syllables] are in faith; having entered the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the immortal oblation is offered. The Person (*puruṣa*) is the size of a thumb. Two [syllables] are "vāṅ ma āsan.
